nameStory: The one-eyed centipede gets its unusual name from having just a single simple eye (called an ocellus) on each side of its head, unlike many other centipedes that have clusters of multiple eyes. This gives it a distinctly different appearance from its many-eyed cousins, making it look almost cyclops-like when viewed head-on.
description: The one-eyed centipede is a small, slender arthropod that's part of the diverse world of soil-dwelling predators. Like all centipedes, it has a flattened, segmented body with one pair of legs per segment, typically ranging from 15 pairs in total. This species is relatively small compared to the large house centipedes you might see scurrying across basement floors. It spends most of its life hunting tiny prey in the dark spaces between soil particles and under leaf litter.

idTips.label: Single eye on each side
idTips.description: Look for just one simple, dark eye spot on each side of the head rather than clusters of multiple eyes - this is the key feature that gives this species its name

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Much smaller than the common house centipede, with a delicate build that feels fragile if gently handled with tweezers or a magnifying glass

idTips.label: Pale coloration
idTips.description: Body appears whitish to pale yellowish-brown, lacking the bold stripes or darker patterns of many other centipede species

idTips.label: 15 pairs of legs
idTips.description: Count the leg pairs - this species typically has exactly 15 pairs of walking legs, giving it 30 legs total

idTips.label: Soil habitat
idTips.description: Found by carefully sifting through moist soil and leaf litter rather than running across open surfaces

habitat: This centipede lives in the hidden world beneath our feet, dwelling in moist soil and the decomposing leaf litter layer of forests and gardens. Look for it by gently sifting through rich, organic soil in wooded areas, particularly where leaves have been accumulating and breaking down. It prefers areas that stay consistently moist but not waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: Active as soil warms up, hunting small soil invertebrates. Best time to find them by sifting through leaf litter as winter debris decomposes.
seasonality.summer: Most active during warm months, though they stay deep in soil during hot, dry periods. Look in consistently moist areas under logs or in garden compost.
seasonality.fall: Still active as they prepare for winter, often found deeper in soil as surface layers begin to cool and dry.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive and very deep in soil below the frost line, making winter observation extremely difficult in New England.

funFact: Despite being called a centipede (meaning 'hundred feet'), this little predator has exactly 30 legs - and amazingly, it can regenerate lost legs if they're damaged while escaping from predators or accidents!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small, pale centipedes in soil, but the single eye on each side of the head is diagnostic - other small centipedes typically have clusters of multiple eyes that look like tiny dark patches rather than single spots.
contextualKnowledge: This species was first scientifically described in 1844, making it one of the earlier centipedes to be formally named by scientists. The scientific name 'emarginatus' refers to having a notched or indented margin, likely referring to some aspect of its body segments.
compareHints: Since this is the only Lamyctes species recorded in New England, compare it with other small soil centipedes in the region by focusing on the eye arrangement - most other small centipedes have multiple eyes clustered together on each side of the head, while this species has just one simple eye per side. This single-eye feature makes it quite distinctive among New England's centipede fauna.
